If she ever decides to learn to play a stringed instrument, you can safely ignore the idea that all the strings need to be reversed and the instrument held the other way around. In practice, I've always felt I had a great advantage, in that my left hand, with the strength and dexterity, is active on the instrument neck; and my right has a less complex job of strumming or picking.

If she can become comfortable with some method of holding a pen/pencil that doesn't involve scrubbing over what you just wrote, she'll benefit. I speak as one who didn't do that. Pens are much better nowadays, but I spent most of my school years with a blue/black edge to my left palm from smeared ink.

It's worth cultivating a few things right-handed in spite of lefthandedness. Batting right handed at baseball, for instance, though a left handed glove for catching from the start will be a blessing- and almost all handheld electric circular saws come with the blade on the right. You can use it lefthanded, but it works better if you learn to hold and direct it with the right. Safer, too. When teaching a left handed person to use sharp or construction tools, spend more time on how to keep your right hand out of the way of trouble. Even so, there will be trouble. It is a right handed world. All my scars are on the right.

Given the chance, she'll find it much easier to eat at a crowded dinner table if she has one of the left ends of the table, or an end-of-table seat. In the middle of the row, right-hand elbows and left-hand elbows trying to do the same job get pretty tangled up, in my experience. While she's little, it'll be easier to feed her from her right side; your left.

Exactly the sort of tips I hoped for. Maybe I should just have her exclusively write in Hebrew to avoid the smear.

Over the years I became very ambidextrous and learned to write with my right hand, I've often wondered what would have happened if I was encouraged to do things with both hands while I was growing up.

If she ever decides to learn to play a stringed instrument, you can safely ignore the idea that all the strings need to be reversed and the instrument held the other way around.

Great advice for any instrument, really. I'm a lefty who learned to play the guitar right-handed, doing that made it much easier for me to learn and I wasn't restricted to only playing my guitar. I played the drums for a while too and reversed the layout of my set, that turned out to be a very significant hindrance because I'd have swap everything around in my head that I was trying to learn, and because I couldn't play anyone else's set without rearranging it, which is not something most drummers are comfortable with.

Actually, "throws right, bats left" is the most employable for fielding positions in baseball. Left-handed throwers can only play at first base or the outfield positions, while right-handed throwers can play anywhere (they are marginally disadvantaged at first base, but not enough to keep them out of the position). However, since most pitchers are right-handed, batting left gives the platoon advantage most of the time. Pitchers are another matter -- most teams have a LOOGY in the bullpen, the Lefty One-Out GuY, to face off against the other team's David Ortiz type when the game is on the line. A dominant left-handed starter like Clayton Kershaw or Sandy Koufax can easily be the staff ace. Personally I fall into that "throws right, bats left" category, but not because of hand dominance. I have the dexterity to throw with either hand, but my left shoulder isn't up to the task of throwing anything heavy -- darts, rubbish, and small household items I will throw with whichever hand gives me the best line to the target. I hit from the left because I can see the ball better that way, as I have marginally better peripheral vision on my right than on my left. She may likewise find that certain things fall to the right hand because of the dominance of something other than her hand.

If she gets into fencing or fighting, left-handedness is generally a slight advantage because opponents are less prepared to deal with it. For bowling, it means getting to use the side of the lane with the oil pattern not so torn up (usually! I recently saw a match where four of the five finalists were lefties, giving this advantage to the right-hander!).

Cue sports (pool, billiards, snooker): no discernible advantage from either side.

Golf: Phil Mickelson is naturally right-handed but was taught early that having his dominant hand out front would give him a better short game. This doesn't seem to have gained traction with anyone else though, and it generally doesn't make that much of a difference in terms of the cost of buying clubs or anything (except right-handed sets are easier to get used), so go with whatever feels best unless someone else has a specific reason for doing otherwise.

Hockey: It's a weird fact that the majority of players put their dominant hand on top, making most right-handed players into left-handed shooters and vice versa. There's usually a shortage of good right-handed shooters to play that wing, so being a lefty might be an advantage. (I didn't, but I'm pretty much a 60/40 ambidextrous type anyhow, so carrying the stick in my left hand when I skated never bothered me.)

Encourage her to not switch the buttons on the mouse even though she moves it to the other side. This means not having to reconfigure anything in software, and a left click is still literally a left click. Having the mouse on that side is actually an advantage though, as it's right next to the alphanumeric typing area, minimizing the reach. When it's on the right, the cursor pad and tenkey section push the mouse out another six inches or so. Also, data entry is facilitated with the mouse in one hand and the tenkey pad under the other. I actually use a custom layout with the keypad on the LEFT to gain this advantage while keeping the mouse on the right.

As for string instruments, she should play one however it feels most comfortable. With wind instruments, you generally don't get a choice (but woodwinds call for dexterity in both hands anyhow). Piano has fixed assignments for the hands as well. The same goes for orchestral strings because she would be sitting in a section and can't be facing the other way from the rest of them. If she ends up a drummer, she can set them up any way she pleases, but doing it in reverse means not being able to sit in on someone else's kit. (Then again, lots of drummers want their kits "just so" and won't use anyone else's setup no matter which way it's laid out.)

Scissors... this depends on how good she is with the "off hand". If she's adequately dexterous with the right hand, you might want to just get her used to right-handed scissors because left-handed scissors are always special-order items. If she's hopeless, then it's probably better to just accept that she'll need her own tools for certain things other people take for granted.

Why are the rings such trouble? I've heard this before and know they make special lefty bound versions even. What do they do to you?

They get in the way. We lefties already have enough of a problem trying to write in a legible manner since even our alphabet is designed to slant the direction a right handed person writes. Rings block our hand, so the left side of the paper is practically useless to us. We have to scrunch our hands just to get in that area, and as stated before, our hand writing is already horrible to begin with. It will especially be stressful if for some reason she has to learn cursive (which is becoming less popular these days). As a lefty, there is a good chance she will want to be creative.

The same goes for spiral notebooks. Righties don't know the struggle of having a wire coil digging into your fleshy paws as you try to drag your hand across the paper. They make bound notebooks instead of spiral, and those are much more lefty friendly. Admittedly, the glue that holds them together is junk, so you will replace them more often, but they are truly a blessing.

I had a left handed teacher in the 3rd grade, and she helped me a lot with how to hold my pen/pencil so that the words weren't smeared as I write. As stated earlier in this thread, your daughter will probably wind up having a designated place to sit at the dinner table. Left most side of the table is really the only option for us to enjoy a meal comfortably. If it's a booth, there' really only one option for us, the end of the table near the walkway. Otherwise our elbow hits the wall while using a fork, and we have to keep our elbow tucked near the side of our body. It's not pleasant. If we are seated next to a right handed person, our elbows will constantly be fighting for space. I am 33 years old and will take my family to dinner with my folks occasionally. After all this time, they still sit in a way to leave a seat available for me in the right location. It's a small thing, but it makes a world of difference.

Things to remember, desks are designed for right handed people, writing is designed for right handed people, nuts and bolts are designed for right handed people. Depending on what stage of life she is in these things will affect her differently. Have patience with her with these items and things like them. Stuff that seems natural to do for you, might not be for her. Especially righty-tighty lefty-loosey.
Try to ensure she lifts her writing implement when writing things by hand. Otherwise, she'll end up with graphite or ink on the sides of her fingers.

A website was in and of itself not meant to be a revenue stream. It was meant to be a means to make money from selling your products and services. Now that we've lost touch with that concept, the common belief is that the web deserves money just for existing. I don't believe that and I wish people would just go back to paying the cost of business on their own while making money on real things instead of views and clicks. Traffic could be so much less if a site didn't have 10 advertising networks running per page bringing their analytics, media and tracking garbage too so the cost would then be lower and consumers would be happier and safer. No one in their right mind would expect to get paid for someone viewing an ad in the newspaper so why did we change when the ad went online? The model is broken.

TL;DR: Ad agencies killed the unobtrusive ads and paying for servers/bandwidth are part of the cost of doing business.

My company operates a website. Our website has had unobtrusive in-page advertisements for a while. Recently, it started emitting pop-up and pop-under advertisements, which generated a large amount of complaints to customer service from users, and were even so obnoxious that our development organization began complaining... they were actually interfering with our developers' ability to develop the website.

The response from marketing was that "they were making us gobs of money" (paraphrased), and that they had already decided not to stop the pop up ads, but would revisit the decision at the next budget deliberation.

Apparently, they work and print money. And I suppose they will stay until somebody comes up with data demonstrating the long-term harm - but even then, there's likely to be a turning point up until which the pop-up ads are still profitable, and I suspect marketing will keep them in place until that point.

Much like the counter-argument to anti-piracy measures, the people that are savvy enough to run adblock are people that were unlikely to ever respond to obnoxious advertising in the first place.
